title: Lifting the anathemas (1965)
hook: Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras lift the mutual excommunications from the old split between East and West

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vatican II, and a pope who wanted fresh air in the church. Your line was open the windows. Which window did you open, even a crack? Day nine hundred sixty-four.

Two churches, one statement, read aloud on the same day in two cities. In Rome, at the end of the council, in front of the bishops. In Istanbul, the old Constantinople, in the patriarch's church. The statement is about something that happened long before anyone in either room was born. Back at the time of the great split between the Christian East and the Christian West, envoys from Rome and the patriarch in Constantinople had pronounced sentences of excommunication on each other. Those sentences had sat on the record ever since, like a door slammed and never reopened. Now Pope Paul the Sixth and Patriarch Athenagoras of Constantinople agree to lift them. Today, two churches saying sorry.

An anathema is a solemn curse or ban, a sentence that puts someone outside the church. The word is in the New Testament. When Paul writes to the Galatians about anyone who preaches a different gospel, the King James Bible gives it as "let him be accursed." Strong words, meant for serious cases. The story usually told of the old split runs like this. Envoys from Rome, in Constantinople, laid a document of excommunication on the altar of the great church there, and walked out. The patriarch and his synod answered with excommunications of their own. The quarrel had many roots, theology, authority, language, politics, and those sentences became a symbol of all of it. Then two men decided to act. Paul and Athenagoras had already met and embraced in Jerusalem. Now they issued a joint declaration. In it they said they regretted the offensive words and the hurtful actions of that time, and they asked that the sentences be removed from memory and from the midst of the church, consigned to oblivion. What it did not do matters too. It did not restore full communion. The two churches still do not celebrate the Eucharist together, and their dialogue continues, with patience, on both sides. The declaration itself says this gesture is not enough to end the differences. It was a start. Jesus put the order of things plainly, in the King James Bible: "Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift." The story goes that the old sentence from Rome was laid on an altar. The undoing began when both sides laid it aside.

Here's the practice: undo one old grudge. Settle, and breathe. Let one old grudge come to mind. Not the biggest one. A medium one. A cousin, an old friend, a former boss. Notice how long you've kept it on the record. Notice what it costs you to keep it there. You don't have to make up with them today. A pope and a patriarch didn't fix everything in one statement either. Just ask: what would it mean to lift the sentence, even if nothing else changes yet? If you pray, you can bring Jesus's words about leaving the gift at the altar. The bell holds the time.
Lifting the anathemas. The joint act in which Pope Paul the Sixth and Patriarch Athenagoras removed the old excommunications between Rome and Constantinople.
Your line: nine hundred years undone. Today, take one step on an old grudge: a short message, a kind word, or simply deciding to stop rehearsing it. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Delegations from Rome and from the patriarchate in Istanbul now visit each other on their churches' patronal feast days, and official dialogue between the two churches continues.

fork.setup: you're a church leader. an old sentence against another church has sat on the record for a very long time. both sides still disagree on real things. what do you do?
options: leave it; nothing can be done until every question is settled.
lift the old sentence together, and keep talking about the rest.
issue a new sentence to match.
fork.reveal: Paul and Athenagoras lifted the sentences together and said the gesture was not enough on its own. the deeper questions are still being worked through.

original.note: Greek, in Galatians 1:8: a thing set under a curse; the King James renders it 'accursed'.

trapdoor: what you thought: the day the great split between East and West ended.
what it means: a pope and a patriarch lifted the old excommunications and expressed regret, without yet restoring full communion.

what a scholar hears: the old sentences fell on particular men, the envoys and the patriarch, not on whole churches; the joint declaration asked that they be removed from memory, a gesture its signers said was not enough on its own.

notes: The carry 'nine hundred years undone' is the index's; the voice gives no dates or counts. The script hook field drops the index hook's year '1054' under the claims rule; the title's year is the index's.
The Joint Declaration is paraphrased (regret for offensive words and hurtful actions; remove from memory and from the midst of the church; consign to oblivion). Confirm wording.
The account of the legates laying the bull on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the synod's counter-excommunication, is hedged as 'the story usually told'; confirm.
Paul VI and Athenagoras met and embraced in Jerusalem before the declaration; confirm.
Read the same day in Rome (at the council) and in Istanbul (the Phanar); confirm. 'Both churches describe the declaration as a beginning' — confirm, or soften.
howItsDone: exchanges of delegations on the feasts of Sts Peter and Paul and St Andrew; confirm.

Editor pass: 'both churches describe it as a beginning' replaced with what the joint declaration says (the gesture is not sufficient to end the differences), in teach, fork reveal and trapdoor; 'old sentences were laid on an altar' corrected to the one Roman sentence, hedged as 'the story goes'.

Editor pass 2: 'do not share the Eucharist' made precise ('do not celebrate the Eucharist together'; Catholic law allows some sharing in limited cases); 'most serious cases' superlative cut; unclear closing line rewritten; howItsDone narrowed to the Rome and Constantinople delegations on patronal feasts.

Audit: hook said 'each side' excommunicated 'the other', implying whole churches; corrected to the envoys and the patriarch excommunicating each other (the 1054 sentences were personal, not church-wide), and the trapdoor's scholar floor now says so; confirm.
